In order to examine whether the outputs of the DL-based methods can be made physically plausible, I performed an additional post-docking energy minimisation of the ligand structures in the binding pocket for the PoseBusters Benchmark set (Figure 2.7).
Again, striped bars indicate predictions with RMSD ⩽ 2 Å while solid bars indicate which of those are also PB-valid i.e., pass all PoseBusters tests.

The figure shows that post-docking energy minimisation significantly increases the number of physically plausible structures of the DL-based methods DiffDock, DeepDock, TankBind, and Uni- Mol but does not improve the poses predicted by AutoDock Vina and GOLD.
I also performed energy minimisation on the Uni-Mol results for the minimal 6 Å pocket (Appendix B, Figure B.19).
The number of poses that pass the tests increases to about the same level as DiffDock.

The fact that energy minimisation is able to repair many of the DL methods predicted poses and increase RMSD ⩽ 2 Å performance shows that at least some force field-defined physics is missing from DL-based docking methods.
An example of a predicted pose that was fixed is shown in Figure 2.8.
However, even with the energy minimisation step, the best DL-based docking method DiffDock still performs worse than the classical methods GOLD and AutoDock Vina.

In this chapter, I discuss PoseBusters, a test suite designed and built to identify chemically inconsistent and physically implausible ligand poses predicted by protein-ligand docking and molecular generation methods.

I show the results of applying the PoseBusters test suite to the output of seven different docking methods, five current DL-based docking methods (DeepDock, DiffDock, EquiBind, TankBind, and Uni-Mol) and two classical docking methods (AutoDock Vina and GOLD).
As mentioned earlier, none of the DL-based docking methods assessed here yet outperforms classical docking methods when both physical plausibility and binding mode RMSD is taken into account.

Our work demonstrates the need for physical plausibility to be taken into account when assessing docking tools because it is possible to perform well on an RMSD-based metric while predicting physically implausible ligand poses (Figure 2.2).

Using the tests in the PoseBusters test suite as an additional criterion when developing DL-based docking methods will help improve methods and the development of more accurate and realistic predictions.
In addition, the individual tests in the PoseBusters test suite highlight docking-relevant failure modes.
The results show that Uni-Mol, for example, predicts non-standard bond lengths and TankBind creates internal ligand clashes.

As mentioned earlier, the ability to identify such failure modes in predicted ligand poses makes PoseBusters a helpful tool for developers to identify inductive biases that could improve their binding mode prediction methods.
Our results also show that, unlike classical docking methods, DL-based docking methods do not generalise well to novel data.

The performance of the DL-based methods on the PoseBusters Benchmark set overall was poor and the subset of the PoseBusters Benchmark set with low sequence identity to PDBbind 2020 General set revealed that DL-based methods are prone to overfitting to the proteins they were trained on.

Our analysis of the targets with sequence identity lower than 30 % to any member of PDBbind 2020 General set revealed that across all of the DL-based docking methods almost no physically valid poses were generated within the 2 Å threshold.

The most commonly-used train-test approach for building DL-based docking models is time-based, e.g., complexes released before a certain date are used for training and complexes released later for testing.
Based on our results, I argue that this is insufficient for testing generalisation to novel targets and the sequence identity between the proteins in the training and test must be reported on.
Post-docking energy minimisation of the ligand using force fields can considerably improve the docking poses generated by DL-based methods.
However, even with an energy minimisation step, the best DL-based method, DiffDock, does not outperform classical docking methods like GOLD and AutoDock Vina.
This shows that at least some key aspects of chemistry and physics encoded in classical docking methods and force fields are missing from DL models.

The PoseBusters test suite provides a new criterion, PB-validity, beyond the traditional “RMSD ⩽ 2 Å” criterion to evaluate the predictions of new DL-based methods, and hopefully will help to identify inductive biases needed for the field to improve docking and molecular generation methods, ultimately resulting in more accurate and realistic predictions.

The next generation of DL-based docking methods should aim to outperform standard docking tools on both RMSD criteria and in terms of chemical consistency, physical plausibility, and generalisability.
This chapter introduced the PoseBusters test suite which can check the generated output of docking methods for chemical consistency and physical plausibility.

The main results from our analysis of five DL-based docking methods are that no DL-based method yet outperforms standard docking methods when considerations of physical plausibility are taken into account, that the DL-based docking methods tested do not generalize to novel data, and that force fields contain docking specific information that is lacking from these DL-based docking methods.
The PoseBusters test suite is a new standard to test for physical plausibility alongside native binding mode accuracy.

Since the publication of the results in this chapter (Buttenschoen et al., 2024), many new DL based docking models, but more broadly also other molecular modelling software, like co-folding methods (Abramson et al., 2024; Boitreaud et al., 2024; Krishna et al., 2024; Wohlwend et al., 2024) and de novo molecular generation methods (Buttenschoen et al., 2025; M. Li et al., 2025) have been assessed using the PoseBusters test suite.

The tests have become a tool for method developers to check that their methods do not egregiously violate stereochemistry and physics, and have helped identify the inductive biases still required to improve DL-based docking methods, as shown by recent improvements (Corso et al., 2024).
Since the publication of the first version of the PoseBusters software, additional tests have been added and bugs have been fixed based on suggestions and feedback from various users.
Maria Kadukova contributed settings for a non-flatness test for aliphatic rings.
Guy Durant identified a bug that prevented passing molecule objects into the main function.
In addition, checks for the connectedness of molecules, the absence of radicals, and clashes with water molecules have been added.
Various stability improvements were made for users running the PoseBusters checks on extremely wonky molecules produced by de novo molecular generators.
Other publications have also advanced assessments of protein-ligand models beyond the metrics mentioned here.

For example, Errington et al. (2025) have expanded the set of metrics by monitoring the conservation of intermolecular interactions, showing another way to possibly improve DL-based protein-ligand models, namely by training models directly to learn intermolecular interactions.
This chapter assessed DL-based methods for docking.
The next chapter takes a look at the data behind those models, its quality, the patterns within it, and what that might actually tell us about how good DL models can be.
All data sets had some failure cases.
The test set with the highest percentage of passing structures was PoseBusters (99.4 %), followed by Astex Diverse PB (91.7 %), and PDBbind 2020 General R1 (78.3 %).
The training set PDBbind 2020 General R1 had 63.0 % passing structures showing an improvement over PDBbind 2020 General (54.5 %).

Table 3.2 summarises the results grouping the intermolecular, intramolecular, and identity checks together; the individual test passing rates are provided in Appendix C. The largest category of errors were intermolecular (e.g. protein-ligand clash) followed by intramolecular (e.g. sanitisation of the ligand).

The commonly used training data set PDBbind 2020 General General contains 19 443 protein- ligand complexes (unique PDB identifiers) and 86.6 % (16 832) passed the intermolecular checks, 69.9 % (13 600) passed the intramolecular checks, and 54.5 % (10 590) structure passed all test (Table 3.2).

The greatest failure modes, as shown in Figure 3.1, were sanitization (2825, 14.5 %), protein-ligand clash (1860, 9.6 %), mismatching molecular formulas (1099, 5.6 %), and clashes with water molecules (732, 3.8 %).
Not all ligands in this data set had entries in the CCD because 2611 ligands are represented as multimers of CCD entries, for example sugars and small peptides.

The PDBbind 2020 General R1 set had similar failure modes (Figure C.5b), but more structures passed overall (67 %, 12 804) than for PDBbind 2020 General (54.5 %, 10 590); this improvement was mainly due to lower failure rates in the RDKit sanitization test, while the number of protein-ligand clashes remained the same.
The CASF-2016 set, a subset of the PDBbind 2020 General set, contained 285 protein-ligand complexes and 263 (91.2 %) passed all tests (Figure C.4).
The failure modes of the MOL2 ligand and PDB receptor files were mismatches in molecular formula (10, 3.5 %), ligand internal strain (5, 1.8 %), and stereochemistry mismatches (5, 1.8 %).
Two (0.7 %) entries failed due to protein-ligand clashes (1O3F, 4TMN).
The results for the other file types are summarised in Table C.1; none of the MOL2 receptor files could be loaded correctly and the SDF and PDB files yielded 4.2 % passing structures.
The Astex Diverse set contains 85 complexes, and 51 (60 %) passed all checks (Figure C.2a).

29 (34 %) complexes did not sanitise, two (2.4 %) had internal clash (1JD0, 1T9B), one (2.2 %) had a mismatching molecular formula (1GM8), and two (2.4 %) had double bond stereochemistry mismatches with the CCD (1S19, 1YVF).

For the recreated Astex Diverse PB set 79 (93 %) complexes passed all checks (Figure C.2b), one (2.2 %) failed due to internal clash (1JD0), one (2.2 %) failed due to internal strain (1YGC), two (2.4 %) had double bond stereochemistry mismatches with the CCD (1S19, 1YVF), and three (3.6 %) had tetrahedral chirality mismatches with the CCD (1GPK, 1S3V, 1OF6).

Further inspection of the files revealed that the MOL files were missing charges which the RDKit does not fill in, and as a result the sanitisation fails, for example for molecules with four-valent nitrogens.
The structures of the other data set that was used to assess docking models in the previous chapter, PoseBusters, pass most tests.
306 (99 %) of the 308 ligand poses pass all the tests (Figure C.1).
There are two failure cases, one protein-ligand clash (7T0D) and one aromatic ring that is not flat (7V3S).
Lastly, the DockGen data set contains 330 protein-ligand complexes.
Inspection of the identifiers reveals that there are two protein-ligand complexes (6XB3, 6O70) that are both in the validation set and in the test set.
None of the complexes pass the tests because there is no bond information in the PDB files (Figure C.3a) and the RDKit does not automatically retrieve this information from the CCD.

Using PyMOL to insert the bonds using the CCD and saving the ligands as SDF files fixes this problem (Figure C.3b) but this approach does not fully create chemically correct RDKit molecule objects: 102 (31 %) ligands fail the RDKit sanitization check and 73 (22 %) fail the InChI inter-convertibility check.
The intermolecular failure modes are 25 (7.2 %) protein-ligand clashes and two occasions (4ZO7, 6MT9) where the ligand is more than 5 Å away from the protein.
The severity of the protein-ligand clashes and the intramolecular ligand clashes in the data sets is shown as box plots in Figure 3.2.

The majority of complexes in all data sets pass both tests; however, the training data set PDBbind 2020 General and the testing data set DockGen set contain outliers with severe clashes of both kinds.
Next, the training data are compared against the predictions made by the models trained on it.
Recall that the five DL-based methods were all trained on most of the PDBbind 2020 General set (Chapter 2, Table 2.2).
The PoseBusters test results of the poses generated by the DL-based docking methods from Chapter 2 are recapitulated in Table 3.3.

Although most of the complexes in the PDBbind 2020 General training data pass the tests, most of the predicted poses of the DL-based models fail the intermolecular tests (Table 3.3), in particular because they contain protein-ligand clashes and intramolecular ligand clashes (Figure C.7).

Figure 3.3 further shows that on the more difficult PoseBusters Benchmark set, more than three quarters of the predicted poses have protein-ligand clashes; this is a much higher rate than observed in the training data.
First, I consider what the results show in regards to the ‘garbage in, garbage out’ hypothesis.
As the results show, the PDBbind 2020 General training data set does have a large number of structures that do not pass the tests.
The most severe structural failure mode is protein-ligand clash (Appendix C, Figure C.6a).
This is shared with the five previously benchmarked DL-based models that were trained on subsets of the PDBbind 2020 General General set (Chapter 2, Table 2.2).
However, when comparing failure rates of the methods (Figures C.7 and C.8) to those in the data sets, I observe higher failure rates (Appendix C, Tables 3.2 and 3.3).

In particular, the methods generate poses with much higher protein- ligand clash rates from the DL-based methods compared to the training data (Figure 3.3) and while the training data does contain systematic structural artefacts, these data issues alone cannot explain the observed error rates in the predicted poses.

In conclusion, there is some evidence that these DL-based models learn protein-ligand clashes from the data, but the quality of the training data does not fully explain the much higher failure rates observed in the models.
To discern the influence of problematic data on model performance, it is not sufficient to examine the training data alone.
One could retrain the models on filtered clean versions of the training data set to see what the effect of the faulty data really is.
However, it is likely that incorrect handling and loading of the data might have caused some of the models to learn from faulty molecular representations.
Indeed, the results show that loading molecular data sets with the RDKit is not trivial.
Depending on which files are chosen and on what options are used, one might get 91 % passing protein-ligand complexes or none when loading the molecules of the CASF-2016 data set.
In general, there is no molecular file type from which the RDKit is guaranteed to load valid molecules.

All file formats admit underspecified or wrong molecular data, and the RDKit parser, as noted, although known for particularly strict parsing, cannot follow the unwritten conventions of other software when dealing with omitted information.
When the RDKit cannot sanitise a molecule, an error is raised.
However, when no error is raised, a molecule can still be wrong.
This is because sanitization does not guarantee that the molecule was correctly loaded.
These silent bugs are logic errors, and they cause molecules to be parametrised wrongly.
This happens when loading the CASF-2016 files.

When loading the SDF files of the ligands instead of the MOL2 files, there are some sanitisation errors, but other ligands load without error but have radicals, non-flat double bonds, and flat non-aromatic rings and their internal energies are much too large (Appendix C, Figure C.4).
This happens despite the two molecular file formats containing identical coordinates and atom types.
The reason is that two different molecules end up being loaded by the RDKit: one is correct, and the other is incorrect.
The wrong chemical representation causes a faulty parametrisation of the UFF in the energy ratio test, leading to a downstream error caused by the file being misinterpreted by the RDKit.

Clearly, the chemical representation of the molecules matters a lot, and much care must be taken to load molecules correctly with the RDKit, because learning from chemically faulty data possibly limits the methods’ performance.

In summary, special care must be taken when loading molecular files with the RDKit - some substructures, such as four valent nitrogens, are never correctly loaded and could lead to systematic blind spots.
Obtaining the latest data from the PDB in mmCIF format and regenerating the data set, as was done for the Astex Diverse, was successful.
The molecular structures loaded from the original files with RDKit were only 60 % PB-valid, but the recreated Astex Diverse set was 92 % PB-valid.

It is apparent that high quality filters (e.g. maximum resolution of 2.5 Å), for example those used to select structures for the Astex Diverse set, the CASF-2016 set, and the PoseBusters Benchmark set, did indeed yield higher quality data selections, even though the PoseBusters tests were not used directly as criteria.
As the PDB continually expands and the RDKit is continually improved, regenerating the data sets periodically will be important.
For future work, it would be interesting to study the diversity and uniqueness of the data.
The PDBbind 2020 General contains 19 443 protein-ligand complexes from the PDB, of which 155 are redundant leaving 19 288 complexes.
For training generative models, it is important not only to have diverse data that do not repeat, but also to have data that cover as much of the input space as possible.
Describing the distribution of the data in terms of diversity measured by protein sequence identity or ligand similarity will be important.
Further work for understanding the trade-off between using all data and selecting only high quality data would be a useful step.

This is because showing that the training data have the same failure modes as the models is only a necessary but not sufficient condition to show that the models have learnt the problems from the data.
Retraining the models with cleaner data would allow this to be measured.
It would be interesting to see what effect retraining the DL-based docking methods on cleaner data sets would have.
This would give a signal of whether efforts to improve the structure models of the PDB, via refitting the models on the electron densities, could be worthwhile for model developers.
In conclusion, the results showed that data sets of molecular structures obtained from the PDB should be carefully inspected, filtered, and errors corrected.
Although the failure modes of the DL-based docking methods resembled those of the training data, I find that the training data were of better quality than the model predictions would make us believe.
To fully discern the influence of problematic data on model performance, the models could be retrained on filtered versions of the data set and their results be compared.
Further, I recommend that all practitioners benchmark and carefully select the training data they choose to build DL-based docking models, maybe less is more in some cases.

Overall, 232 665 unique pairs of PDB structures with ligands bound to the same protein and the same binding pocket were collected, and 53 048 (23 %) of these are pairs of identical ligands bound to the same receptor (but still in different PDB structures).
Of the 179 617 pairs containing non-identical ligands, 99 319 (55 %) pairs contain fragments, 3698 (2.1 %) pairs are elaborations, and 2587 (1.4 %) contain fragment elaborations.
Further, 92 255 (51 %) of the non-identical pairs contain drug-like molecules and 46 159 (26 %) pairs contain a pair of a fragment and a drug-like ligand.
Binding poses are more commonly conserved in pairs of chemically similar ligands.

Figure 4.1 shows the shape and pharmacophoric similarity, measured by SCRDKit , of all pairs of non-identical pairs of ligands (179 617) versus chemical similarity, measured via chemical fingerprints.
The plot shows that, for more chemically similar pairs of ligands, the binding pose is conserved more commonly.
It also shows a high similarity of H-bond interactions (yellow) for chemically dissimilar ligands.
Figure 4.2 shows the same set of non-identical pairs (179 617) binned by chemical similarity and in terms of the percentage of poses conserved (SCRDKit ≥ 0.8).
This plot shows the trend more clearly; clearly, there is a steady increase in the percentage of poses conserved as a function of chemical similarity.
For ligand pairs with chemical similarity larger than 80 %, around 90 % of the observed pairs in the data set have conserved binding modes.
Of the 53 048 pairs of identical ligands, 99.0 % are pairs that conserve the binding mode (SCRDKit ≥ 0.8) and 1.0 % (527) do not conserve binding mode (SCRDKit < 0.8).
Six of those pairs of structures containing identical ligands (identical CCD identifiers) with non-conserved poses are shown in Figures D.3 and D.4.
Three of these poses are distinctly different (Figures D.3a and D.4c and Section D.4).

The publications of the PDB structures reveal that ligand DGT in structures 4TNX and 4TO6 is an allosteric binder, ligand DIF binds is shown in different species (6HN0 is ovine and 6HN1 is caprine serum albumin), and ligand OCF receptors 8AYJ and 8ONN differ by a point mutation.
This might explain some pairs of poses scoring lower than expected (Figure D.3b).
Similarly, three of the pairs of ligands with identical CCD identifiers have have non-identical Fingerprints (2048-bit ECFP4 Tanimoto similarity less than 1, for example Figure D.4c).

The ECFPs (2048-bit, radius 2) used here also distinguish ligands with different protonation patterns, resulting in some ligand pairs with identical CCD identifiers scoring less than one in terms of fingerprint similarity.

Fragments, typically small organic molecules with molecular weights less than 300 Da, are sometimes used as starting points for drug discovery.
It has been reported that fragments can adopt multiple poses in the same binding site.
Plots showing the distributions of pose similarity for identical ligands (53 048) split into fragments and non-fragments are shown in Figure 4.5.
They show no difference between fragments and non-fragments in this subset, 99.7 % of fragments, and 99.4 % of non-fragments conserve their pose.
For the non-identical pairs, the percentage of conserved poses versus chemical similarity is plotted in Figure 4.6; the line for all pairs shown in Figure 4.2 is provided for reference in grey.
For chemical similarity between 20 % and 70 %, there is slightly higher pose conservation than in all pairs, whereas in between 70 % and 100 % there is lower pose conservation.
Overall, the results do not show significant differences in fragments versus all pairs in the collected data.
Malhotra and Karanicolas (2017) found that in 86 % of 297 pairs of assembled smaller and larger ligands the binding mode is conserved upon chemical elaboration.
Figure 4.8 shows pose conservation as a function of chemical similarity for ligand pairs where one ligand is the substructure of the other.
Across all bins of chemical similarity, pose conservation is higher than for all pairs, as shown by the reference line for all pairs.
For elaborations with chemical similarity of at least 50 %, more than 80 % of poses are conserved.
Next, I tested whether elaborations starting with fragments behave differently.
As shown in Figure 4.7 this is not the case; elaboration and fragment elaborations preserve poses at similar rates.

For both of these analyses, the number of pairs for the bins of high chemical similarity is relatively low, with less than 30 examples of fragment elaborations of chemical similarity of at least 80 %.
One common elaboration strategy is to grow molecules a few atoms at a time.

Figures 4.9 and 4.10 shows the proportion of conserved poses as a function of the difference in the number of atoms for all pairs in Figure 4.9 and for fragment elaborations Figure 4.10, for pairs with up to 20 atom-difference.
For pairs with up to 13 atoms difference, the percentage of poses preserved is more than 80 %.
It appears that the MCS between the smaller and larger elaborated ligand in our data set maintains its pose very frequently.

My analysis shows that chemical similarity correlates strongly with pose conservation, as shown in Figures 4.1 and 4.2.
This agrees with the approach often used in structure-based drug design.
Small changes in molecular structures often maintain the binding modes of the original structures more often than larger ones.
In particular, elaborations of molecules maintain binding modes very often; more than 80 % of all observed elaborations maintain the binding pose.
This agrees with the main principle of structural medicinal chemistry, that is making small changes to lead compounds and existing scaffolds.

The statistic that 99.0 % identical ligands conserve their binding pose in the same pocket of different PDB structures confirms how consistent the binding events observed in the crystal structures are.
However, the remaining pairs (1.0 %, 527) include pairs with significant changes in the binding mode when bound to the same receptor (Section D.4).

Slightly different protonation patterns affected the ECFP4 fingerprints, but spot checks revealed that point mutations, difference in pH of the crystal, re- ceptors from different species, and allosteric binding might cause these differences.
The 90 % sequence identity threshold for pairing protein receptors does not filter pose-relevant point mutations.
Identical fragments have been observed elsewhere to adopt multiple binding poses (Malhotra & Karanicolas, 2017).
Initially, perhaps surprisingly, in our data, pairs of identical fragments have a high rate (99.7 %) of pose conservation.
However, this does not mean that fragments do not adopt multiple poses, because in our pair selection process, I only choose the combination of ligand poses that leads to the highest SCRDKit .
When there were multiple fragments in a binding site, I chose the pair with the pose that was the most similar.
This explains the high rate of pose conservation in identical fragments.
Fragment elaboration pairs showed a similar high rate of pose conservation as all elaboration pairs.
The trends observed for the MCS also agree with intuition: If more of a ligand is conserved, and if fewer atoms are added, then the more similar the smaller and larger ligand poses are.
However, the fitted model on smaller ligand size, relative MCS size, and number of atoms added only explained about 33 % of the variance observed in pose similarity (Pseudo 𝑅2 = 0.33).
The missing variation might be explained by the amount of chemical complementarity removed and added, which was not represented in these models.
Intermolecular interactions are directly related to binding affinity.

For this reason, medicinal chemists count interactions and add up their contributions when designing structures, as can be gleaned from average interaction strength tables (Burnell et al., 2016, Table 3.1, p. 32).
The correlations between interactions and pose conservation were lower than expected.
Almost no positive correlation is observed (Figure 4.13); the hydrogen bond interaction type has the highest Spearman correlation, which is almost negligible at 𝜌 = 0.08.
This suggests that pharmacophores and interactions contain orthogonal information and should both be considered when designing.

The data set used in this study has a positive selection bias, as I have selected pairs of protein-ligand complexes for which experimentally resolved structures of both ligands bound within the same pocket of the same protein exist.
A modification of a molecule that failed to lead to a binding event in the same binding site (or did not bind at all) would not be represented in our data.
Another bias in our study is that the chemical space represented here is the one explored by structural experiments that led to the submission of structures to the PDB.
These experiments do not explore the proteomic and chemical space uniformly, and only a very small subspace of combinations of ligands and proteins can ever be explored.
A further limitation of this analysis is that most PDB structures do not contain biologically accurate protonation patterns of receptors and ligands.
Similarly, the hydrogen bonds in water networks of binding sites are mostly unresolved in experimental structures.
Although I know that the solvation and protonation patterns strongly contribute to protein-ligand binding, I did not have the data to analyse these here.
In this chapter, I conducted a study of the protein-ligand binding patterns of pairs of structures of similar ligands bound to the same pocket in the same protein from the PDB.
My analysis shows that ligands with high chemical similarity conserve binding modes more frequently and that elaborations, on average, conserve poses more frequently.
Interaction metrics are found to correlate with chemical similarity, but not with pharmacophoric measurements.
This chapter provided some insight into the types of biases that medicinal chemists use when performing structure-based drug design.
It also provides a large data set for the study of protein-ligand patterns that can be further explored.
In the next chapter, I use a diverse subset of these paired data to steer a DL-based docking model to conserve user-chosen interactions and substructures.

The re-docking experiments show that physical plausibility can be improved to the same extent by a post-prediction energy minimisation, by post-prediction with the simple force field, guidance with the simple force fields, and guidance with molecular dynamics.
Figure 5.3 shows a comparison of the failure modes of DiffDock-L, DiffDock-L with post-prediction energy minimisation, and guidance with the simple clash terms.
The figure shows that energy minimisation and physical guidance have virtually the same effect: The physical validity is mostly improved due to reducing protein-ligand clashes.
A full list of our experiments re-docking the cognate ligand into the rigid receptor in the PoseBusters data set is provided in Table 5.2.

Guidance with OpenFF 2.0.0 and the simpler clash terms yield the same improvement in accuracy and physical validity (45.8 ± 2.9 % RMSD within 2 Å and PB-valid) as the post-prediction minimisation (45.8 ± 2.8 %) applied to DiffDock-L (26.6 ± 2.5 % RMSD within 2 Å and PB-valid).
Performing the post-processing minimisation before or after the scoring makes no difference.
The forward guidance (45.8 ± 2.9 % RMSD within 2 Å and PB-valid) and reverse guidance (45.1 ± 2.8 % RMSD within 2 Å and PB-valid) schemes perform equally well.

However, forward guidance, which differentiates through the model, takes more time (2 min per protein-ligand complex) than the reverse guidance scheme (1.3 min), both significantly longer than DiffDock-L (12 s).

Table 5.2 also shows that, as expected, providing the centroid location of the docked ligand through guidance improves the accuracy (63.6 ± 2.8 % RMSD within 2 Å) over DiffDock-L (51.9 ± 2.8 % RMSD within 2 Å).
Providing the centroid and running the clash terms results in the overall highest accuracy and physical validity (59.7 ± 2.8 % RMSD within 2 Å and PB-valid).
However, even though the poses are now all within 5 Å RMSD, the 2 Å RMSD threshold is satisfied by only 63.6 % of the generated poses.
Those poses failing this threshold have the centroid in the right location, but the binding pose is still not correct.
In our cross-docking experiments, ligands are docked into the crystal structure of the paired ligand, and not the cognate receptor structure.
The results for cross-docking on the Malhotra set are visualized in Figure 5.5 and summarized in Table E.3.
On the Malhotra data set (n=297), the raw performance of DiffDock-L is 27.7 % (RMSD within 2 Å and PB-valid poses).
Using only clash terms (‘simple physics’), the performance of GuideDock is 58.2 % (RMSD within 2 Å and PB-valid poses).
This increase is due to the physical validity metric increasing from 32.8 % to 81.2 % despite accuracy dropping from 79.7 % to 66.8 %.
For comparison, GOLD without constraints generates 16.0 % PB-valid poses within 2 Å RMSD on this data set.
The main failure modes that remain are RMSD being too large (79.7 %) followed by too small protein-ligand distances (3.9 %).
With region constraints using the oracle fragment information, the performance rises to 33.6 % PB-valid poses within 2 Å RMSD.
The main failure modes remain RMSD being too large (58.3 %) followed by too small protein-ligand distances (7.8 %).
Finally, the alignment via protein chains does lead to clashes with the receptor and only 41.0 % of generated protein-ligand poses are PB-valid.
This is mostly due to protein-ligand clashes 51.9 % but also 5.5 % of the large ligand crystal conformations have too much steric strain and do not pass the internal energy check.
The results for cross-docking on the GuideDock (n=148) are shown in Figure 5.6 and summarized in Table 5.3.
Docking the modified ligands into the rigid receptors of the related ligands DiffDock yielded 22.3 ± 3.4 % PB-valid poses within 2 Å RMSD.
Adding simple physics guidance increases this number to 33.8 ± 3.9 %.
Adding binding site information in terms of a centroid in the guidance further increases the performance to 51.0 ± 4.1 %.
In comparison, GOLD without constraints and a spherical binding site with a radius of 25 Å yields 55.6 ± 4.1 % PB-valid poses within 2 Å RMSD.
Adding atom-wise region constraints for the substructure information increases the performance of GOLD to 71.4 ± 3.7 %.
The baseline alignment via the protein chains yields less PB-valid poses (66.9 ± 3.9 %) than GuideDock (71.6 ± 3.7 %) or GOLD 92.4 ± 2.2 %, due to the generation of more clashes with the receptor.
For a chemical series of molecular glues (Cereblon E3 ligase modulators, also known as immunomodulatory imide drugs), the substructure of the ‘anchor’ is believed to be highly conserved in place.
Adding position constraints for this highly conserved motif successfully guides and recapitulates the binding mode, as shown in Figure 5.7.

The resultant performance is shown in Figure E.2 (Appendix E).

Overall, the guidance improved the prediction accuracy by 10 % from around 49 % (DiffDock-L RMSD within 2 Å) to 59 % (GuideDock RMSD within 2 Å).
By implementing simple guidance in DiffDock-L, I demonstrated that the predictions of diffusionbased molecular structure models can be steered in a controlled manner.

Using simple loss functions for guidance was sufficient to increase the physical plausibility of generated poses, as evaluated by PoseBusters, while avoiding the expensive parametrisation required for energy minimisation with a full molecular dynamics force field.
I further showed that guidance improves the performance of DiffDock-L not only in terms of phys- ical plausibility but also in accuracy, as measured by RMSD within 2 Å.

Incorporating prior information from related ligands, sometimes referred to as templates, unsurprisingly improved performance for cross-docking, but only when the underlying assumptions of this approach were satisfied.
Crucially, this requires that the imposed constraints do not interfere with docking and that the rigid receptor does not sterically block the correct ligand pose.
Using guidance to enable pocket-specific and constrained docking was shown to work well in practice.
Revealing additional information about the ligand and its binding pose to the model during inference improved performance relative to the base model.
I showed that the same base model can be applied across these different tasks.
However, when compared to the classical docking method GOLD, our models still performed worse in terms of physical plausibility, though not in terms of RMSD accuracy.
Training the base model to generate only PoseBusters-valid poses may therefore be a promising direction.
Overall, the performance of the resulting method, GuideDock, is at best comparable to that of the classical docking method GOLD, both with and without additional constraints.
A more fundamental paradigm shift, such as moving from docking to co-folding, may be required to surpass traditional physical docking methods in a meaningful way.
Our approach uniquely demonstrates how physical terms derived from force fields and userdefined biases can be integrated with state-of-the-art DL methods for rigid small-molecule docking.
The terms used here improve results by incorporating information that the model either did not learn to exploit (physics) or did not have access to (user biases).
Introducing user biases also enables practitioners to directly test their hypotheses within the docking process.
In this chapter I presented GuideDock, a DL-based docking method that innovates by adding diffusion guidance to the DiffDock-L blind docking method.

This allows reusing the pre-trained model to perform constrained docking and pocket-specific docking, while simultaneously also improving the physical plausibility of the generated poses in comparison to the unguided DiffDock.

Although GuideDock does not surpass classical docking methods, in particular the classical docking method GOLD, the experiments demonstrate that repurposing a single blind docking model for multiple different tasks is possible.
Since I started working on GuideDock, other researchers have implemented guidance terms in biological structure prediction models.
The ‘steering’ approach that was added to the second version of the preprint of Boltz (Wohlwend et al., 2024) this summer is very similar to our method.
I am excited that I was on the right track with this work, but I suspect that the machine learning community now views co-folding as having superseded docking.
The aim of this thesis was to investigate deep learning (DL)-based protein–ligand docking.

Motivated by the landmark success of AlphaFold2 in protein structure prediction and by the observation that DL- based docking has not yet achieved a comparable impact, I sought to contribute to the advancement of this field.

In particular, this work aimed to assess the current capabilities of existing methods, identify opportunities for improvement, and support the maturation of DL-based docking as a practical technology.
My research improves our understanding of DL-based protein-ligand docking by investigating the shortcomings of common evaluation metrics, training data, and testing setups.
In addition, my research explored the interplay of physics-based and DL-based approaches and showed that diffusion guidance can inject physical biases and user knowledge.
My first key finding is that the established RMSD metric of being within 2 Å of the crystallographic binding mode is insufficient to assess DL-based protein-ligand docking.
Using examples, I showed that the 2 Å RMSD threshold admits physically impossible pretzel-shaped conformations and stark protein- ligand clashes, among others.
As a remedy, I implemented a new metric, PB-validity, which consists of a series of physical and chemical plausibility tests.
This new metric has been adopted by the research community to benchmark docking, de novo molecular generation, and co-folding models.
My most significant contribution is that I have systematically shown that DL-based docking methods have not yet outperformed classical docking methods.
I did this in two independent ways: first, by creating a new, more difficult test set, the PoseBusters test set; and second, by introducing the new metric: PB-validity.
Both provide unique insights into the performance of the models: The PoseBusters tests enumerate chemical and physical failure modes, telling the user what exactly has gone wrong and how badly.
Independently, using a novel out-of-distribution training data test set and splitting it by sequence identity revealed that DL-based methods generalise less well than classical docking methods.
The impact of this contribution has seen a renewed effort of model developers to improve the physical plausibility of docking as well as co-folding models.

Also important is my finding that the very training data, the crystal structures in the PDBbind 2020 General set (and its successor PDBbind 2020 General R1), are polluted with the same failure modes with which DL-based methods struggle.
Filtering, pre-processing, or remediating the training data is rarely done but should be; this includes double-checking that the molecular representations loaded from the data sets are correct.
A simple way to do this is to use the PoseBusters tests also to inspect the training data, but that alone does not guarantee problem-free structures.

Regarding time-based training-test data splits, I found that time-splits are insufficient to demonstrate generalisation because they omit use case-dependent considerations of target and pocket similarity, ligand similarity and known binding modes of congeneric series, and interaction conservation.

Splitting my test set by maximum sequence identity to the training data, I showed that DL-based models perform much better close to the training data and worse on more dissimilar proteins–using the entire PoseBusters tests set without subdivision captures only average performance, which is the weakness of time-based splits.

The lesson for practitioners is to consider receptor sequence identity, interaction similarity, ligand chemical similarity, and pocket similarity of protein-complexes of interest and report such metrics on data splits when benchmarking protein-ligand structure prediction methods.
My thesis also makes a methodological contribution.
The usefulness of guidance for adding physical and user biases to diffusion-based structure models is shown.
The GuideDock approach provides a convenient interface for influencing model predictions via force fields, already familiar to practitioners.
I show that any force field term can be used including soft constraints and clash terms.
GuideDock demonstrates that guidance can improve the physical validity of the predictions and allow the user to define a binding site and substructure constraints.
The same principles are applicable to co-folding methods as well.
I have also shown that the DL-based models analysed here have not yet learnt (neither explicitly or implicitly) some of the rules encoded in the force fields.
This suggests that physics and DL-based methods might still be combined successfully.
I demonstrated two ways of doing this: (i) adding an energy minimisation after pose prediction; and (ii) using diffusion guidance with physics-inspired terms.
Both improve the physical plausibility of the generated poses of the methods.
Further ways of combining force fields and diffusion models are easy to think of and should be explored.
Another practical contribution to the field are two new docking test sets.

The first is the PoseBusters test set that includes data both similar to and different from the training data (PDBbind 2020 General), to highlight the current shortcomings of DL-based models and the way they are benchmarked.
The second is the GuideDock test set, which contains pairs of protein-ligand complexes of small molecules that adhere to the same binding pockets on the same protein chain.

The PoseBusters Benchmark set has already been adopted by the scientific community as a test set; the GuideDock set will no doubt be useful for testing template-based and constrained protein-ligand prediction methods.

Finally, I quantified the relationship between the chemical similarity of related ligands and the similarity of their binding poses; this relationship was found to be even stronger for chemical elaborations of smaller ligands.

This finding is of particular relevance to medicinal chemists, as it provides an empirical basis for the substructure constraints used in constrained docking and, more broadly, in fragment-based drug design.

subsection: 6.2 Limitations and recommendations for future research
text: Other workflows using DL-based docking will follow soon.
My research has explored and helped improve both DL-based docking and co-folding methods, especially in terms of chemical and physical plausibility.

It has also shown that DL-based protein-ligand docking has not yet reached its potential; however, personally, given the current rate of progress, I believe that DL-based approaches are very likely to become competitive within three years.

I am delighted to have contributed directly to the field by adding new metrics, tools, and benchmark test data sets, providing insights into training data, model performance, different ways to guide diffusion- based models, and ultimately a new guidance model.
